My land in Quzhou has always grown winter wheat and summer maize. My father grew them, I grew them, and I will grow them again this year. I know these crops. I know how they look when they are sick, when they are thirsty, when the nitrogen is not enough. I do not need to experiment at my age.

My contracted land is about 5 mu. My sons are both in the city now. I manage it myself, though my wife helps during harvest. At 73, I cannot do as much as I used to, so I hire a neighbor with a tractor to do the rotary tillage in autumn before I sow the wheat. For the maize in June, I just direct-seed after the wheat comes off — no need to plow again.

For the wheat, I will put down the base fertilizer before sowing — diammonium phosphate and urea mixed in — then topdress with urea at the jointing stage. This is what everyone does here. I irrigate at sowing, at winter dormancy, at jointing, and at heading. Four times. The well water is still accessible. My yield has been around 430–450 jin per mu most years, so I expect the same.

For the maize, I buy hybrid seed from the county supply cooperative — the same Zhengdan 958 I have used for many years. I know this seed. I fertilize once at planting and once when the plant is knee-high. Summer rain usually helps, but I irrigate once if July is dry. Maize is easier on me physically.

I keep half a mu for vegetables near the house — garlic, cabbage, some beans — just for the family table. I do not count this as a cash crop.
